{{Short description|Lemma describing the behaviour of pseudo-orbits near a hyperbolic invariant set}}
In the [[Dynamical systems theory|theory of dynamical systems]], the '''shadowing lemma''' is a [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] describing the behaviour of pseudo-orbits near a [[Hyperbolic set|hyperbolic invariant set]]. Informally, the theory states that every pseudo-orbit (which one can think of as a numerically computed trajectory with rounding errors on every step<ref>{{MathWorld | title = Shadowing Theorem | urlname =  ShadowingTheorem }}</ref>) stays uniformly close to some true trajectory (with slightly altered initial position)—in other words, a pseudo-trajectory is "shadowed" by a true one.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hammel |first1=Stephan M |last2=Yorke |first2=James A |last3=Grebogi |first3=Celso |title=Numerical orbits of chaotic processes represent true orbits |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |series=New Series |date=1988 |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=465–469 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1988-15701-1 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-19/issue-2/Numerical-orbits-of-chaotic-processes-represent-true-orbits/bams/1183554729.full|doi-access=free }}</ref> This suggests that numerical solutions can be trusted to represent the orbits of the dynamical system. However, caution should be exercised as some shadowing trajectories may not always be [[physically realizable]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chandramoorthy |first1=Nisha |last2=Wang |first2=Qiqi |date=2021 |title=On the probability of finding nonphysical solutions through shadowing |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0021999121002849 |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |language=en |volume=440 |article-number=110389 |arxiv=2010.13768 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2021.110389|bibcode=2021JCoPh.44010389C |s2cid=225075706 }}</ref>

== Formal statement ==
Given a map ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;''X'' of a [[metric space]] (''X'',&nbsp;''d'') to itself, define a '''&epsilon;-pseudo-orbit''' (or '''&epsilon;-orbit''') as a sequence <math>(x_n)</math> of points such that <math>x_{n+1}</math> belongs to a &epsilon;-neighborhood of <math>f(x_n)</math>.

Then, near a hyperbolic invariant set, the following statement holds:<ref>{{cite book |first1=A. |last1=Katok |first2=B. |last2=Hasselblatt |title=Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontomo0000kato |url-access=registration |location=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1995 |isbn=0-521-34187-6 |at=Theorem 18.1.2. }}</ref> 
Let &Lambda; be a hyperbolic invariant set of a [[diffeomorphism]] f. There exists a neighborhood U of &Lambda; with the following property: for any ''&delta;''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 there exists ''&epsilon;''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, such that any (finite or infinite) &epsilon;-pseudo-orbit that stays in U also stays in a &delta;-neighborhood of some true orbit.
:<math>
\forall (x_n),\, x_n\in U, \, d(x_{n+1},f(x_n))<\varepsilon \quad \exists (y_n), \, \, y_{n+1}=f(y_n),\quad \text{such that} \,\, \forall n \,\, x_n\in U_{\delta}(y_n).
</math>

==Popular culture==
In [[Men at Arms]] (1993), a novel by [[Terry Pratchett]], the "Shadowing Lemma" appears as a fictional creature that "exists in only two dimensions and eats mathematicians." In the same passage, Pratchett also references the "quantum weather butterfly," a nod to the [[butterfly effect]] and chaos theory.
